title: Tracking Proteasome Degradation: A Cross-Organ Analysis via Intact degradomics Top-Down Mass Spectrometry
projectDescription: Identifying the peptides generated by the proteasome is essential for understanding its role in regulating critical cellular processes such as apoptosis, signaling, and immune responses. In this study, we introduce an enzymatic top-down mass spectrometry approach that allows real-time monitoring of proteasome-mediated cleavage, providing detailed insights into substrate degradation patterns. By examining proteasomes from different organs, we reveal organ-specific peptide production and degradation behaviors, offering a deeper understanding of how proteasome subtypes affect cellular function. This method is well-suited for investigating the influence of proteasome regulators, inhibitors and activators, on proteasome activity. Additionally, its versatility makes it applicable to other proteolytic complexes, paving the way for further research on proteostasis systems.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Immediately prior to the degradation assay, α-synuclein and 20S proteasomes from different organs were buffer exchanged by bio-gel P-6 columns (BIO-RAD 7326227) to 10 mM ammonium acetate. α-synuclein (final concentration of 7.5 µM) was mixed with 20S proteasome (final concentration 0.5 µM) on ice and then incubated at 37 °C for different time points (0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 min or 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min). After the indicated time points, aliquots were quenched with formic acid (final concentration 5%), before snap freezing in liquid nitrogen. Samples were stored at -80 °C until measurement. All experiments were performed in three replicates. All samples for intact degradomics MS were measured on an UHMR Orbitrap Instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany). To utilize this instrument for the analysis of low molecular weight peptide fragments, ion optics and mass were externally calibrated with cesium iodide solution (concentration 2 mg/ml) in low mass and ion transfer mode and Quadrupole isolation calibration was performed with Pierce Triple Quadrupole Calibration Solution Extended Mass range (#88340). Samples were transferred to the instrument by electrospray ionization from in-house prepared gold-coated borosilicate capillaries with the following instrument tune settings operating in positive ion mode: Spray voltage 1.2 kV, capillary temperature 250 °C. Ion optic settings were used in the default modus for low m/z ion transfer target with S-Lens RF level 100 V and trapping gas pressure set to 1. For enzymatic top-down samples, ions were collected for IT max 750 ms and AGC target of 5e6 over a scan range from 450 to 2,000 m/z. All spectra were acquired at resolution 200,000 over an acquisition period of 5 min. For Native MS analysis, in-house purified α-synuclein, myoglobin and cytochrome c purchased from Merck (M1882 and C2506) were measured on an UHMR Orbitrap Instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany). 3µl of Sample was sprayed to the instrument as descried above. Sample solutions were in 10-200mM Ammonium Acetate, at 10µM, 2µM and 7.7µM for α-synuclein, myoglobin and cytochrome c, respectively. Spray voltage was 1.2 kV, capillary temperature 250 °C. Ion optic settings were used in the default modus for low m/z ion transfer target with S-Lens RF level 200 V and trapping gas pressure set to 0.3. Ions were collected for IT max 500 ms and AGC target of 5 x 106 over a scan range from 1000 to 4,000 m/z. HCD of 1 or 65 was used only for native measurement of α-synuclein or MS/MS for Top-Down analysis and ProSight Lite software48 was used for fragment mapping. All spectra were acquired at resolution 50,000 over an acquisition period up to 3 min. A set of peptides were selected for validation using standard top-down mass spectrometry. Precursor ions were isolated using a window of 5 m/z and HCD energy was applied until a complex fragment spectrum was provided (typically 25 to 35V). The spectra were acquired at resolution 200,000, over a scan range from 450 to 2,000 m/z. The acquired spectra were deconvoluted by applying the Xtract algorithm integrated to the FreeStyle software suite with default settings. Orthogonal to the ClipsMS software, ProSight Lite software was used for fragment mapping.
dataProcessingProtocol: Spectra were averaged over the entire acquisition period (5 min). Deconvolution was performed using the Xtract algorithm (FreeStyle v/ 1.8.63.0). All ions were allowed with no threshold for intensity or minimum number of detected charges across the entire scan range. Except for the fit factor settings, all Xtract options were kept as default. As output, mass of MH+ was selected. The resulting monoisotopic mass and intensity lists were either directly used for ClipsMS peptide mapping (C-terminal peptides/ y-ions) or further adapted to treat proteasome-generated peptides as top-down fragments (Internal and N-terminal peptides/ by internals and b-ions). To achieve this, the molecular weight of a water molecule (18.010565 Da) was subtracted from the monoisotopic mass list. ClipsMS was then executed with a 10 ppm error tolerance for terminal and internal fragments. Peptides were mapped against the full-length α-synuclein sequence (UniProt accession number P37840), with a minimum fragment size of 4 amino acids. No additional modifications were included, and the software was configured to identify b-, y-, or by- fragments based on the input files. For subsequent data analysis, only peptides identified in at least two out of three replicates were considered. Raw data processing was performed in Excel and python. Peptide plots, Split violin plots, and density plots were performed in the python environment. Furthermore, freely available online sources were utilized for Upset plots and Venn diagrams. Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad prism and Perseus software suite.
